title: Motion with weight: linear, eased and spring
description: Why some animations feel alive and others feel mechanical. An interactive lab with the three curves and the squash that adds weight, using the Clint carousel as an example.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: Aura and the agents that appear in this tutorial's carousel.

blocks.text: You know that feeling that an animation is "off", but you can't say why? Most of the time it's not the duration or the color. It's the curve. The way the thing speeds up and slows down.
In this tutorial I put the three curves side by side so you can feel the difference yourself, and I show the two weight rules I used in the Clint carousel. Shall we?

Linear means constant speed. It starts already running and stops all at once. Nothing in the real world moves like that, which is why the eye finds it odd. It's what AI delivers when nobody says anything. Linear only makes sense for things that are truly mechanical, like a clock hand.
Eased: speeds up and slows down

The eased curve starts slow, speeds up in the middle and slows down at the end. It already feels much more natural. It's great for things that just change position without arriving anywhere: a light streak sliding in the background, a ruler drawing itself.

A spring speeds up, overshoots the target just a tiny bit and comes back. That's how an object with mass stops. I used a spring on everything that arrives: the messages on the phone, the cards, the CTA pill. The rule was damping 0.8, which gives at most a minimal bounce. More than that turns into a cartoon, and that's not the tone of a sales brand.

blocks.label: The spring used in the carousel

blocks.text: A detail that makes a difference: this spring is a formula, not a simulation. It responds only to time. That fits what we saw in the first tutorial: the same instant always produces the same frame.
Why the frame depends only on time:
When a bubble lands, it squashes 6% and bounces back. It gets wider by the same amount it gets shorter, to keep its volume. Nobody notices it consciously, but everyone feels it.

An element that sits still for too long looks frozen. The phone moves up and down 10 pixels over the whole slide, on a sine wave that closes perfectly with the loop. It's not animation, it's breathing.

blocks.caption: The same slide, with the same timing. Only the curves changed.

items: Something that arrives or appears: spring.
Something that only changes position or color: eased.
Something truly mechanical, like a counter: linear.
Something still for more than 2 seconds: a very small breath.
A click: the button sinks about 5% and comes back in under a quarter of a second.

blocks.text: So, which curve do you use most today? If the answer is "the tool's default", try changing just that in your next prototype. It's the cheapest change with the biggest effect I know of in motion.
